summary: Most travelers to the DR Congo need a visa in advance — the official eVisa (evisa.gouv.cd) for arrivals at Kinshasa, an embassy visa, or a sponsor-arranged "visa volant" on arrival, and a yellow fever certificate is mandatory for everyone. The east of the country is an active conflict zone.

payments.text: US dollars are the de facto second currency. Bring crisp, undamaged bills printed 2009 or later, as older or torn notes are refused everywhere. Cards work only at top Kinshasa hotels; Congolese francs are used for small purchases and mobile money is growing.

safety.text: Governments advise against all travel to eastern DRC — North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri, where the M23 conflict and other armed groups are active — and to much of the rest of the country. Kinshasa itself sees high crime and occasional unrest; travel with experienced local support.

bestTimeToVisit.text: June to September is the dry season in Kinshasa and the south — the best window for city visits and the Congo River; the vast country spans the equator, so seasons flip between north and south.

tips.text: Do not travel to eastern DRC — North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri are active conflict zones with fighting between the army, M23 and other armed groups; Goma and Bukavu have both been directly affected.
Your yellow fever certificate is checked on arrival and frequently again on departure. Keep it with your passport for the entire trip.

Bring US dollars in crisp, unmarked bills printed 2009 or later — damaged or older notes are refused by banks, hotels and traders alike. Small denominations are handy, and change often comes in Congolese francs.
Never photograph airports, ports, bridges, borders or anything official or military — travelers are regularly detained over photos; ask before photographing people.
The DRC spans two time zones: Kinshasa and the west run on UTC+1, while Lubumbashi and the east run on UTC+2. Check which applies to your itinerary.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for the Democratic Republic of the Congo?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes — nearly every nationality needs a visa in advance, either the official eVisa (evisa.gouv.cd), a visa from a DRC embassy, or a sponsor-arranged "visa volant" on arrival. Only a handful of African countries have waiver arrangements.

faq.question: How does the DRC eVisa work?
faq.answer: Apply on the official portal, evisa.gouv.cd, with your passport, photo and hotel or invitation details. The eVisa is geared to arrivals at Kinshasa's N'djili airport — if you are entering overland or at another airport, confirm it is accepted there or use an embassy visa instead.

faq.question: What is the "visa volant"?
faq.answer: A visa issued on arrival, but only when a sponsor inside the DRC has obtained prior authorization from the immigration service (DGM) before you fly. It is used by business travelers and organized tours; you cannot simply turn up and buy one.

faq.question: Is the yellow fever vaccine mandatory for the DRC?
faq.answer: Yes. A yellow fever certificate is required for all travelers aged 9 months and over, checked on arrival and often on departure too. Without it you can be refused entry or vaccinated on the spot.

faq.question: Is the DRC safe to visit?
faq.answer: Large parts are not. The east (North Kivu, South Kivu, Ituri) is an active conflict zone under do-not-travel advisories, and crime is high even in Kinshasa. Trips that do go well are typically organized visits to Kinshasa and the west with experienced local operators.

faq.question: Do East African Community citizens need a visa for the DRC?
faq.answer: The DRC joined the EAC in 2022 and visa facilitation for EAC citizens is being phased in. Some travelers report eased or waived requirements, but application is not yet uniform. EAC passport holders should confirm current treatment with the DGM or a DRC embassy before traveling.
